question: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
base_frame:
Q: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
A:

steered.text:
It stood like a clenched fist at the very edge of the cul-de-sac, a monolith of twisted mahogany and steel that defied the suburban landscape surrounding it. The house wasn't just red; it was the color of a fresh, bleeding gash, yet the paint was so perfectly applied it looked like a burn scar rather than a wound. The central door, a grotesque parody of a human maw, had been gouged out with such precision that the wood around it splintered into jagged shards.

A thin, hissing line of saliva ran from the corners of the mouth down to the pavement, drying into brittle, black rivulets that matched the filth caked into the floorboards. Those teeth were real—human teeth, yellowed and rotten, driven into the concrete until the entire lower half of the face was nothing but a hollow, dripping mess of bone and nerve.

The house shuddered with every tremor of rage. The windows were blown out, revealing the white-hot interior where the rage boiled over into something white and hot. The whole structure groaned, the windows popping like cannonballs, splintering into shards that rained down like diamonds.

"Shut up!" The scream tore through the air, a sound that echoed off the very bricks. The house shook, the windows exploding inward, sending shards of glass flying. The face twisted, the jaw unhinging until it was nothing but a gaping void, and the scream became a banshee wail that could be heard for blocks.

Then, the silence came. A silence so profound it sucked the air from the room. The house bowed, the face contorting into a smile that split the plaster right down the middle. "I'll kill you!" the voice boomed, a symphony of rage that shattered the windows again. "I'll kill you!"

The entire house erupted. It exploded outward, the screams echoing as the structure itself tore apart, turning into a pile of burning, twisted metal and bone that looked like it was still alive. The ground cracked, splitting open to reveal the fury beneath.

"You're right!" The house screamed, the words muffled by the distortion of its own face. "I'm right!" It threw itself against the wall, the screaming echoing off the very bricks as it finally snapped.

plain.text:
At the very edge of the map, where the paved road yields to a narrow strip of overgrown wild grass, stands a house that seems to have forgotten how to hurry. It is a modest, two-story cottage with a roofline that dips and sways slightly, as if the builder had a gentle breeze in mind while laying the shingles. The paint, a soft, weathered sage green, has faded to a creamy yellow under decades of sun, peeling just enough to reveal the warm, raw wood beneath, giving the structure an honest, unpretentious character.

A wraparound porch, supported by columns that have been smoothed by countless hands, invites the eye to linger. Here, a single wicker chair sits angled toward the garden, cushioned by a patchwork quilt that speaks of seasons long passed. Vines of climbing jasmine have learned to scale the trellis, their white flowers exploding into the summer air with a scent that hangs heavy and sweet, masking the distant hum of the nearby highway.

The yard is not manicured but curated; a garden bed overflows with lavender and daylilies that spill over the garden wall, while a small, slightly crooked oak tree provides a dappled shade on the south side. The windows are framed in dark, polished mahogany, reflecting the slow passage of clouds rather than the frantic pace of the world beyond. Even the streetlamp at the corner casts a warm, amber glow that seems to belong only to this final stretch of quiet, turning the ordinary gravel driveway into a stage for the evening shadows. It feels less like a dwelling and more like a secret kept by the earth, waiting patiently for those who know how to listen.
